items.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022
items.q: It was me, Mike and Sanborn and a great trombone player, Wayne Andre. We showed up at the session... So it became our job to write a chart.

ctx.x: And if it was not professionally done then you had to do some scrambling? © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Well yeah, we had to do some writing sometimes, and on some very good records. This one always comes to mind, on “Born to Run” the Bruce Springsteen record. It was me, Mike and Sanborn and a great trombone player, Wayne Andre. We showed up at the session and there was music paper on our stands but they were blank. And I think they might have had some bar lines but sometimes they didn’t even have bar lines. So it became our job to write a chart. And this was a little out of our — I’ll never forget it — “Tenth…
This is very interesting for me because I’ve played that song with different bands so to hear that thing and remember that I’ve played [scats]. That’s great.

items.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002
items.q: As a matter of fact I was a nobody on the band compared to Randy Brecker and Faddis and those people.

ctx.x: I’ll bet. Was that a scene or what? A different kind of Benny Goodman scene?

No it was totally different. I mean there was a lot of love between the musicians in that band. There was a lot of camaraderie. Benny had a lot of musicians kind of divided in the band too you know. There was a lot of love in the musicians and there was a lot of love for Jaco, it’s just that I mean Jaco was just Jaco. He was just a crazy person. I mean like Jaco took his bass threw it in a lake in Japan, and he did it so the Japanese people would go diving for it and get it back. That’s how much vanity he had.…
